outputs.L1:
JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) — An Indonesian court has sentenced Abu Dujana, the alleged military commander of an al Qaeda-linked terror network, to 15 years in prison.

Dujana is suspected of plotting attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott Hotel in Jakarta. He is the alleged leader of the military wing of Jemaah Islamiyah, a group believed to be linked to al Qaeda and committed to creating a Muslim “superstate” across much of Southeast Asia.

A slight, wiry man, Dujana is accused of direct involvement in the 2002 Bali nightclub bombings, which killed more than 200 people, most of them Western tourists. He is also suspected of plotting later attacks on the Australian Embassy and the J.W. Marriott Hotel, both in the Indonesian capital.

Authorities further allege that Dujana was behind violence in Poso, on Indonesia’s eastern Sulawesi island, where fighting between Muslims and Christians periodically erupts and sometimes turns deadly. Police have accused Jemaah Islamiyah of sending armed militants to the region.

On Monday, the court found Dujana guilty of illegally possessing firearms and explosives and of harboring suspected terrorists. His lawyers said they may appeal the sentence.

Following his arrest last June after a four-year manhunt, Dujana admitted to CNN that he was Jemaah Islamiyah’s military chief. However, he said he assumed that role only after the attacks on Western targets.

He described Jemaah Islamiyah to CNN as “an underground organization,” saying that “it will continue to exist and continue to move on with its plans” to create an Islamic state under Sharia law, despite his capture.

“When a part of it is cut off ... there will be a replacement, it’s only natural,” he said.

Dujana denied involvement in the Marriott Hotel attack. He told CNN that he had helped fugitive suspect Noordin Top plan the attack and had met him both before and after the devastating blast, which killed 12 people and injured 150.

“It’s true, I did have a meeting with Noordin before the Marriott bombing, but that doesn’t mean I was involved in the attack,” he said. “In that meeting, we’re just aligning our views with each other — there was absolutely no discussion about planning any bombing.”

In his CNN interview, Dujana was quick to express messages of hatred, calling all Westerners legitimate targets because of the actions of leaders such as U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whom he accused of denying Muslims the chance to be in power.

Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan from 1988 to 1991. He told CNN that he met al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the fight against Soviet occupation. At the time, Dujana said, bin Laden was a field commander and he was an ordinary soldier.

Dujana said bin Laden was highly respected then and had helped him and others come to believe that it was permissible to kill people in defense of Islam.

“I didn’t read it in the Quran,” he said. “It’s based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics, especially what Osama bin Laden first said.”

“Because of America’s arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it’s permissible to kill American soldiers. It’s halal; it’s permitted,” he said.

The court also declared Jemaah Islamiyah a terrorist organization Monday and ordered it to pay 10 million rupiah, or $1,088.

Around the time Dujana was captured last June, authorities also apprehended Jemaah Islamiyah’s leader, known simply as Zarkasih. A verdict in his case is expected soon.

Last week, two other senior Jemaah Islamiyah figures — Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim — were brought to Indonesia following their arrest in Malaysia. Both are being investigated for their possible role in fomenting violence in Poso.

Terrorism expert Sidney Jones said Abdur Rohim is believed to have replaced Zarkasih as the leader of Jemaah Islamiyah.

“It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be,” Jones told CNN by e-mail last week. “It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future.”

CNN’s Kathy Quiano contributed to this report.

Dujana was arrested last June after a four-year search. Following his capture, he acknowledged to CNN that he had served as Jemaah Islamiyah’s military chief, though he said he took that role only after attacks on Western targets had already occurred.

In an interview with CNN, he called Jemaah Islamiyah “an underground organization” and said it would continue operating and pursuing its objective of creating an Islamic state governed by Sharia law, despite his arrest.

“When a part of it is cut off ... there will be a replacement, it’s only natural,” he said.

Dujana rejected accusations that he took part in the Marriott hotel bombing. He told CNN he had assisted fugitive suspect Noordin Top in planning the attack and had met him both before and after the bombing, which killed 12 people and wounded 150.

“It’s true, I did have a meeting with Noordin before the Marriott bombing but that doesn’t mean I was involved in the attack,” Dujana said. “In that meeting, we’re just aligning our views with each other — there was absolutely no discussion about planning any bombing.”

During the CNN interview, Dujana voiced hostile views toward the West, saying all Westerners were valid targets because of the policies of leaders such as U.S. President George W. Bush and then-British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whom he accused of denying Muslims the opportunity to hold power.

Dujana studied in Pakistan and fought in Afghanistan between 1988 and 1991. He told CNN he encountered al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in Afghanistan during the war against Soviet occupation. At that time, he said, bin Laden was a field commander, while Dujana was an ordinary fighter.

According to Dujana, bin Laden was highly respected then and influenced him and others to believe that killing could be justified in defense of Islam.

“I didn’t read it in the Quran,” he said. “It’s based on the teachings of our teachers, clerics, especially what Osama bin Laden first said.”

“Because of America’s arrogance, many in the Muslim world know, believe, it’s permissible to kill American soldiers. It’s halal; it’s permitted,” he added.

On Monday, the court also formally designated Jemaah Islamiyah as a terrorist organization and fined it 10 million rupiah, equivalent to $1,088.

Around the time Dujana was arrested last June, authorities also detained the leader of Jemaah Islamiyah, who is known simply as Zarkasih. A ruling in his case is expected soon.

The previous week, two other senior Jemaah Islamiyah figures — Dr. Agus Purwanto and Abdur Rohim — were returned to Indonesia after being arrested in Malaysia. Both are under investigation over suspected involvement in stirring violence in Poso.

Terrorism analyst Sidney Jones said Abdur Rohim is believed to have succeeded Zarkasih as Jemaah Islamiyah’s leader.

“It is another major blow to Jemaah Islamiyah, but difficult to tell what the impact will be,” Jones told CNN by e-mail last week. “It could embolden a more militant faction. [It] could also lead to some serious reassessment within the organization about its future.”

Terrorism analysts said the conviction was significant because Dujana was believed to have been part of Jemaah Islamiyah’s senior command structure at a time when the group was trying to rebuild after repeated arrests and killings of its operatives.

Indonesia, the world’s most populous Muslim-majority country, has arrested hundreds of suspected militants since the 2002 Bali bombings. counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a chronological news article about Indonesia sentencing Abu Dujana to prison, explaining who he is, what attacks he is accused of helping plan, his comments on Western targets and bin Laden, and the broader impact on Jemaah Islamiyah.
counterfactuals.output:
**Indonesia Sentences Jemaah Islamiyah Commander Abu Dujana to Prison**

**JAKARTA, Indonesia —** An Indonesian court sentenced Abu Dujana, a senior commander of the al-Qaida-linked militant network Jemaah Islamiyah, to prison, marking another major step in Jakarta’s campaign to dismantle the group blamed for some of Southeast Asia’s deadliest terrorist attacks.

Abu Dujana, whose real name is Ainul Bahri, was a former head of Jemaah Islamiyah’s military wing and one of the most important militants captured in Indonesia after the 2002 Bali bombings. Authorities said he helped keep the organization functioning after a series of arrests weakened its leadership.

The sentence followed his arrest in 2007 during a police crackdown on Jemaah Islamiyah cells in Java. Prosecutors said Abu Dujana had sheltered fugitives, helped maintain weapons caches and played a role in the group’s militant operations. He was accused of helping plan attacks including the **2003 bombing of the JW Marriott Hotel in Jakarta**, which killed 12 people, and the **2004 bombing outside the Australian Embassy**, which killed several more. Jemaah Islamiyah has also been blamed for the **2002 Bali nightclub bombings**, which killed 202 people, most of them foreign tourists, though Abu Dujana denied direct involvement in that attack.

During court proceedings, Abu Dujana acknowledged his senior role in Jemaah Islamiyah but sought to distance himself from indiscriminate attacks on civilians. He said Western targets had been viewed by militants as legitimate because of Western governments’ policies in Muslim countries, but he also suggested that bombings killing civilians had damaged the group’s cause. He spoke of Osama bin Laden with respect as a figure who had defended Muslims, while denying that his own activities were simply directed by al-Qaida.

Abu Dujana’s importance stemmed from his long history inside the regional militant movement. Trained in Afghanistan in the 1980s and 1990s, he became a key link between Indonesian militants and transnational jihadist networks. Indonesian officials described him as a disciplined organizer who helped train recruits and preserve Jemaah Islamiyah’s structure after many of its most notorious bomb-makers and field operatives were killed or arrested.

The conviction came amid a broader decline in Jemaah Islamiyah’s operational capacity. Indonesian police had captured or killed several leading figures, including bomb-maker Azahari Husin and other operatives tied to attacks on hotels, churches, nightclubs and diplomatic targets. Analysts said Abu Dujana’s imprisonment further weakened the group’s command structure and disrupted its ability to coordinate large-scale bombings.

Still, security officials warned that the sentence did not eliminate the threat entirely. Jemaah Islamiyah had already begun shifting from spectacular attacks toward recruitment, religious outreach and smaller clandestine networks. The imprisonment of Abu Dujana symbolized Indonesia’s success in breaking up the organization’s most violent wing, but it also underscored the continuing challenge of preventing splinter groups and radicalized individuals from carrying out future attacks.
